Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

without preposition

also with no, without you, without doing, without any

classical

Cic. Fam. 16.10.2: sine tē omnia mea mūta esse
Sen. Ep. 6.4: nūllīus bonī sine sociō jūcunda possessiō est
Traupman 408

sine + abl.

preposition with the ablative

“Without any” is sine ūllō, never sine nūllō. Nōn sine is a favourite understatement: nōn sine pugillāribus, not without my notebooks.

Other words

  • quīn + subj. — without (doing), after a negative: never … without …

    conjunction with the subjunctive, after a negative clause · also used · classical · Cic. Verr. 2.4.95: numquam tam male est Siculīs quīn aliquid facētē et commodē dīcant

    “Without doing” has no single Latin form: after a negative, quīn; elsewhere a participle with nōn, or a second clause with nec.

  • absque + abl. — without (as a plain preposition, post-classical)

    preposition with the ablative · avoid · post-classical · Plaut. Men. 1022: nam absque tē esset, hodiē numquam ad sōlem occāsum vīverem

    In Plautus and Terence only in the condition absque tē esset, had it not been for you (Lewis & Short). As a plain “without” it belongs to later Latin; use sine.

Examples

  • eī cupientī audīre nostra dīxī sine tē omnia mea mūta esse

    when he wanted to hear my work, I told him that without you all my writing was dumbCic. Fam. 16.10.2

  • difficilis facilis, jūcundus acerbus es īdem: nec tēcum possum vīvere, nec sine tē

    difficult and easy, sweet and sour, you are all at once: I can’t live with you, or without youMart. 12.46.1–2

  • sit nox cum somnō, sit sine līte diēs

    may the night come with sleep, and the day without quarrelsMart. 2.90.10

  • nūllīus bonī sine sociō jūcunda possessiō est

    no good thing is a pleasure to have without someone to share itSen. Ep. 6.4

  • Hispānī sine ūllā mōle in utrēs vestīmentīs conjectīs ipsī caetrīs superpositīs incubantēs flūmen trānāvēre

    the Spaniards, without any fuss, stuffed their clothes into leather bags, lay on their shields on top of them and swam the riverLiv. 21.27.5

  • numquam tam male est Siculīs quīn aliquid facētē et commodē dīcant

    things are never so bad for the Sicilians that they don’t say something witty and aptCic. Verr. 2.4.95

  • vēnor aliquandō, sed nōn sine pugillāribus, ut quamvīs nihil cēperim nōn nihil referam

    I hunt now and then, but not without my notebooks, so that even if I catch nothing I bring something homePlin. Ep. 9.36.6
